Custom Calls

Source: vignettes/articles/custom_calls.Rmd
custom_calls.Rmd

Note: Everything in this article is about the default "pjrt" backend.

{anvl} lowers every primitive to a StableHLO program, which XLA then compiles. While the StableHLO opset covers the most common operations, there are cases where one wants to go beyond it, either for efficiency reasons or to exercise more control over the implementation. This is what so-called custom calls are for. Here, we cover the CPU case, and Custom Calls on CUDA focuses on the GPU case.

The StableHLO operations operate on whole arrays. Loops are supported via prim_while(), and scalars are available as nv_scalar(), but a StableHLO loop over scalars has a very different performance profile than an actual C/C++ or CUDA loop. A StableHLO while does not run its body once per element of an array: it runs it once per iteration, on the whole loop-carried state, for as long as its condition returns TRUE (StableHLO spec). Written over the whole array, a loop whose length depends on the element – a series summed until it converges, a continued fraction, a root search, rejection sampling – therefore makes every element go round as often as the slowest one needs. XLA lowers a compiled program into a sequence of thunks, units of work that its runtime executes one after the other, with control flow such as a loop among them (XLA docs). In a simplified view, the body of the loop becomes a compiled unit of its own, which the runtime invokes anew after checking the condition on every iteration. That loop control costs time on every iteration where a C/C++ loop spends a few instructions per iteration. A loop that handles one element at a time pays this cost per element. It also gives up SIMD: a body that works on one scalar has nothing to vectorize, while a while over a whole array vectorizes each step. On CUDA the situation is even worse: every iteration is at least one kernel launch, and a kernel launch costs on the order of microseconds, where an iteration of a loop inside a kernel costs nanoseconds. In C/C++, by contrast, each element stops when it is done. Custom calls can also be advantageous when the computation does operate on arrays but involves hundreds or thousands of small operations. There, XLA is not the problem, but instead the trace-time overhead in R becomes significant. Finally, for common operations, such as linear algebra primitives, hyper-optimized routines exist in LAPACK or cuSOLVER and a generic compiler like XLA cannot match their performance.

The price of a custom call over composing a function of existing primitives is that anvl does not know how to compute its derivative. Also, the custom call cannot be fused with the surrounding StableHLO operations.

We will keep the implemented example simple to focus on the mechanics of the registration and not the numerical routine. Specifically, we will implement the hypotenuse \(\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\). While this can be implemented directly in {anvl}, the custom call will use the numerically optimized routine from <cmath>, namely std::hypot().

Implementing this involves three steps:

  1. Writing the actual function
  2. Registering the function with {pjrt}
  3. Calling the custom call from {anvl}

Step 1: Write the handler

In order to write the handler, we need to import the FFI (Foreign Function Interface) headers from XLA, which are vendored in {pjrt}’s inst/include directory. We will also use Rcpp to interface with R.

// [[Rcpp::plugins(cpp20)]]
// [[Rcpp::depends(pjrt)]]
#include <Rcpp.h>
#include <cmath>
#include "xla/ffi/api/ffi.h"

using namespace xla::ffi;

Because we want our custom call to work with both single and double precision, our hypot_impl will take in the xla::ffi::AnyBuffer type for its arguments and result. Generally, the signature contains one AnyBuffer per argument and one Result<AnyBuffer> per result. hypot_impl itself is a template over the element type T, with which it reads the buffers through typed_data<T>().

Because a handler may be called from XLA’s worker threads, it must not touch R’s C API (no allocation, no Rf_error(), no printing).

// The actual work, once the element type is known.
template <typename T>
static Error hypot_impl(AnyBuffer x, AnyBuffer y, Result<AnyBuffer> out) {
  size_t n = out->element_count();
  if (x.element_count() != n || y.element_count() != n) {
    return Error::InvalidArgument("hypot: operands must have the same size");
  }
  const T *xp = x.typed_data<T>();
  const T *yp = y.typed_data<T>();
  T *op = out->typed_data<T>();
  for (size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
    op[i] = std::hypot(xp[i], yp[i]);
  }
  return Error::Success();
}

do_hypot() then looks at the element_type() of the buffers and calls hypot_impl<T>() with the matching T. The alternative would be a statically typed Buffer<DataType::F64>, which pins the handler to one data type and makes XLA reject all others. Because AnyBuffer moves the type checking from XLA into the handler, typed_data<T>() only asserts that T matches in a debug build, and reinterprets the bytes otherwise. The comparisons of the sizes and of the three element_type()s, and the default: branch, only keep the handler from reading memory it should not. Whether the operands are valid for the computation should be checked in R, before the call: by the inference rule of a primitive, as shown in making it a primitive.

// Dispatch on the dtype; f32 and f64 are what std::hypot covers.
static Error do_hypot(AnyBuffer x, AnyBuffer y, Result<AnyBuffer> out) {
  DataType dt = x.element_type();
  if (y.element_type() != dt || out->element_type() != dt) {
    return Error::InvalidArgument("hypot: operands and result must have the "
                                  "same dtype");
  }
  switch (dt) {
    case DataType::F32:
      return hypot_impl<float>(x, y, out);
    case DataType::F64:
      return hypot_impl<double>(x, y, out);
    default:
      return Error::InvalidArgument("hypot: only f32 and f64 are supported");
  }
}

Next, XLA_FFI_DEFINE_HANDLER_EXPLICIT() attaches the binding specification to do_hypot(), which tells the runtime that it takes two operands and one result, in that order. The macro defines hypot_handler, a plain function pointer.

XLA_FFI_DEFINE_HANDLER_EXPLICIT(hypot_handler, do_hypot,
                                Ffi::Bind()
                                    .Arg<AnyBuffer>()   // x
                                    .Arg<AnyBuffer>()   // y
                                    .Ret<AnyBuffer>()); // hypot(x, y)

Finally, hypot_handler_ptr() hands that pointer to R as an external pointer, which is what the registration function in Step 2 expects. {pjrt} hands its own handlers to R the same way.

// [[Rcpp::export]]
SEXP hypot_handler_ptr() {
  return R_MakeExternalPtr((void *)hypot_handler, R_NilValue, R_NilValue);
}

The loop in hypot_impl() handles one element at a time on one thread, which is where a production kernel goes further. Binding .Ctx<ThreadPool>() hands the handler XLA’s thread pool to split the elements across, and the {highway} package, used through LinkingTo: highway, provides Google’s Highway library for SIMD: one kernel that works on several elements per instruction, compiled for every instruction set of the CPU and picked at run time.

Step 2: Register it with PJRT

pjrt::pjrt_register_custom_call() registers the handler under a target name. That name is a process-global key, so prefix it with something specific to your package – mypkg stands in for its name here. The second argument is one handler per platform, "cpu" (a synonym for PJRT’s own "host") and "cuda". Platforms you leave out simply have no implementation: running the call there aborts with No FFI handler registered for mypkg_hypot.

pjrt::pjrt_register_custom_call(
  "mypkg_hypot",
  list(cpu = hypot_handler_ptr())
)

Step 3: Call it

We will use two right triangles as example inputs:

library(anvl)
x <- nv_array(c(3, 5), dtype = "f64")
y <- nv_array(c(4, 12), dtype = "f64")

nv_custom_call() takes the target name, the operands, and the dtype and shape of each result, which nv_aval() combines into an abstract array. anvl cannot infer the result types – the handler decides them – but nothing forces you to write them out as literals: dtype() and shape() of the operands are available at trace time, so a generic call reads

nv_custom_call("mypkg_hypot", x, y, output_types = nv_aval(dtype(x), shape(x)))
#> AnvlArray
#>   5
#>  13
#> [ CPUf64{2} ]

nv_custom_call() has further arguments for attributes passed to the handler, memory layouts, results written in place of operands, and calls kept for their side effects; see nv_custom_call() for these, and XLA’s custom call guide for how a handler reads its attributes.

Important: A handler that indexes by axis has to keep in mind that R stores arrays column-major, while XLA reads them row-major. Every operand therefore reaches the handler transposed, with all of its axes reversed: an R \(3 \times 2\) matrix A arrives as the row-major \(2 \times 3\) matrix t(A), with dimensions() {2, 3}. The same holds for the result, which the handler has to write transposed: a row-major matrix product, for example, returns A %*% B by computing t(B) %*% t(A). operand_layouts / result_layouts can instead ask XLA to rearrange the data before and after the call, see nv_custom_call().

Making it a primitive

nv_custom_call() is opaque to XLA, and therefore to {anvl}’s differentiation: gradient() will not go through it. It also shows up in a traced graph as a generic custom_call rather than an operation with a name of its own.

Both are fixed the same way – by giving the call its own primitive, exactly as in Adding a Primitive. What is specific to a custom call is the StableHLO rule, which connects the primitive to the handler, so that is all this section shows. A pullback rule, which makes the primitive differentiable, is written as for any other primitive, as described in the pullback rule step of that article.

The inference rule is where the operands are checked now. It runs when the primitive is traced and refuses what the handler cannot take with an R error that names the primitive, before anything reaches XLA, so a handler that is only ever called through its primitive can do without checks of its own. The dtype stays generic here too: the inference rule propagates whatever float dtype the operands were traced with:

prim_hypot <- new_primitive("hypot", function(x, y) {
  infer_fn <- function(x, y) {
    if (!as.character(dtype(x)) %in% c("f32", "f64") || dtype(x) != dtype(y)) {
      cli::cli_abort("{.arg x} and {.arg y} must both be f32 or both be f64.")
    }
    if (!identical(shape(x), shape(y))) {
      cli::cli_abort("{.arg x} and {.arg y} must have the same shape.")
    }
    list(nv_aval(dtype(x), shape(x)))
  }
  graph_desc_add(self, list(x = x, y = y), infer_fn = infer_fn)[[1L]]
})

The lowering rule is handed the output_types that follow from the inference rule. It reaches one level lower than nv_custom_call() does, emitting stablehlo::hlo_custom_call() directly, because a rule is handed FuncValues rather than arrays. Those speak XLA’s order: their shapes are the R shapes reversed, and the layouts are XLA’s, which number the axes of that reversed shape from zero. XLA’s default layout, n - 1 down to 0, is R’s column-major order:

prim_hypot[["stablehlo"]] <- function(x, y, output_types) {
  layout <- rev(seq_along(shape(x)) - 1L)
  list(stablehlo::hlo_custom_call(
    x,
    y,
    call_target_name = "mypkg_hypot",
    api_version = 4L,
    has_side_effect = FALSE,
    output_types = output_types,
    operand_layouts = list(layout, layout),
    result_layouts = list(layout)
  ))
}

Calling the primitive runs the handler:

prim_hypot(x, y)
#> AnvlArray
#>   5
#>  13
#> [ CPUf64{2} ]

Using it in a package

Rcpp::sourceCpp() keeps this article self-contained. In a package, the .cpp file goes in src/hypot.cpp, with {pjrt} in LinkingTo:, and the handler has to be registered in the package’s .onLoad() hook via pjrt::pjrt_register_custom_call().
